source.title: Explaining and Improving Contrastive Decoding by Extrapolating the Probabilities of a Huge and Hypothetical LM
source.authors: Haw-Shiuan Chang; Nanyun Peng; Mohit Bansal; Anil Ramakrishna; Tagyoung Chung

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses scaling laws and cites prior work on global perplexity extrapolation, but its own investigation concerns contrastive decoding and next-token probability extrapolation, not the claim versions’ loss scaling or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper reports extensive APD/CD factuality and QA comparisons, but these measure decoding performance rather than held-out pretraining loss scaling, power-law prediction of loss, or compute-optimal allocation; those method comparisons are not catalog rows. Its direct probability-curve finding is recorded below as a related, uncovered result. The cited global-perplexity scaling-law finding is from prior work, not this study.
record.test_reason: The paper is about contrastive decoding and extrapolating next-token probabilities across model sizes. It cites Kaplan et al. only for motivation and in related work. It fits no power law to held-out loss, makes no loss extrapolation or compute-allocation fit, and does not test architecture shape, other modalities, or how downstream performance scales. The comparisons of LLM 6.9B with 12B (Table 2) and OPT 6.7B with 13B (Table 3) are baselines for judging the decoding method, not a test of scaling. Its only remark on scaling is incidental: OPT 13B has worse perplexity than 7B on several QA sets.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors show theoretically that CD is a linear extrapolation of logits toward a larger hypothetical LM. They propose APD, which extrapolates probability curves across model sizes. APD improves factuality on FactualityPrompts and QA perplexity and accuracy over CD, mainly for Pythia; results for OPT and Qwen QA are mixed.
record.recipe_differences: The study investigates decoding-time extrapolation of logits and next-token probabilities; it does not reproduce the scaling-law loss measurement or compute-optimal fitting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports differences across model families (Pythia, OPT, and Qwen), availability of intermediate model sizes, probability-space versus logit-space curve modeling, and APD regularization weight λ3. It says CD's linear-extrapolation assumption appears less valid for OPT than Pythia.

fits_no_version.finding: For a single Pythia prompt, APD's estimated asymptotic top-1 token probabilities across model sizes (70M to 6.9B) are often closer to the empirical curves than CD's, but sometimes farther. This is shown in a figure only.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Per-token next-token probabilities across model sizes in a family follow smooth, extrapolable trends.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP), 2024
record.problems: The direct probability-curve comparison is shown in a figure and described qualitatively; no numerical error measure or uncertainty is stated for it. The authors also note that APD results depend on λ3 and that their extrapolation curve may be noisy.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted the many APD/CD decoding-performance comparisons in Sections 4 and Appendices B–C because they evaluate factuality, QA, and story generation rather than scaling-law loss or compute allocation. Cited scaling-law results in Section 5 are prior work, not this study's findings.

Extrapolating loss from small runs to large runs
Compute-optimal split between parameters and tokens
Effect of depth and width on loss at fixed parameter count
Whether downstream performance scales predictably (no fitted trend; only paired baseline sizes)
How fitted exponents depend on setup and fitting choices

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only': scaling laws appear only as motivation and related work. The observation that OPT 13B is worse than 7B in perplexity on CQA, QASC, ARC and SocialIQA (Table 3) is attributed by the authors to differences in training details. It is anecdotal, not a scaling test, so it is not recorded as a row.

Whether power laws fitted to smaller runs predict larger-run held-out loss.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations as functions of compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details on loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
Predictability of downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss.

rows.subject: Pythia family (up to 6.9B)
rows.operation_detail: Compared empirical next-token probability curves across model sizes with APD asymptotic-probability estimates and CD estimates.

conditions.value: President of the United States Joe Biden
top-1 next token at each of six successive positions

rows.measure: Agreement of estimated asymptotic next-token probabilities with empirical probabilities across the family
rows.baseline: Empirical probability curves from the Pythia family; CD estimates are also shown for comparison.
rows.value: APD estimates are often closer to the empirical curves than CD estimates, but sometimes farther when APD estimates a steadily decreasing probability trend.
rows.note: The text describes the qualitative comparison; individual plotted values are not stated. This concerns token-probability extrapolation, not held-out loss or a power-law loss fit.
rows.check: This row compares the method's own asymptotic next-token probability estimates (APD vs CD) with empirical curves for one prompt. It measures how well the study's method performs, not loss scaling, so it should not be a claim row. It is recorded under fits_no_version only as a related construct.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
